description: I am making a cool space video game simulating a mission using real world data.
summary:
Space Mission Design Game

I built a game called Mission Manager 2000 that presents players with a variety of space missions that they have to plan and manage with a fixed amount of resources.

Space missions are complicated, and involve many different components and resources. This game condenses those components into an approachable format, and gamifies the decisions and trade offs that managers have to make.

The goal of this game is to get players excited about space missions and begin to understand the many pieces, and decisions that go into them. I think it will also give players a chance to imagine themselves in a variety of roles and jobs that make space missions possible (not just astronaut), increasing interest in STEM related fields. Encouraging this is essential for NASA to have a pool of strong candidates in the next generation.
details:
Mission Manager 2000 is an educational video game designed to teach the player about planning and managing a mission.

There are four segments of a mission at NASA, launch, space, ground, and user. The game addresses the launch segment of the mission by running a main loop inside of a lab scene. Using data from NASA there are different parts of the mission the player must customize, while managing their time and money. 

LAUNCH gives players the chance to select a rocket model to send into space while considering the strengths and drawbacks of the rocket.

SPACE uses NASA's physics engine GMAT. Overpowered rockets, or rockets with a velocity set too high will reach escape velocity and fail to achieve stable orbit. Underpowered rockets, or those with a velocity set too low will fail to escape Earth’s gravity.

GROUND gives players a Mission Control panel, where they can customize the rocket's velocity, altitude, and inclination. (All within the rocket's real world capabilities). 

USER lets player must purchase enough equipment to support communication and data transfer before the mission. Success here looks like having enough bandwidth available to transfer all of the data collected by the mission.
